passages.happening:
God asks Ezekiel, ‘will you judge her? Will you pass judgment on the city of bloodshed?’ (verse 2). He is to confront Jerusalem with her abominations. Her leaders use their power to shed blood (verse 6). ‘Father and mother are treated with contempt. Within your walls the foreign resident is exploited, the fatherless and the widow are oppressed’ (verse 7). The Sabbaths are profaned, slanderers shed blood, and every kind of sexual wrong is done (verses 8-11). ‘In you they take bribes to shed blood. You engage in usury, take excess interest, and extort your neighbors. But Me you have forgotten’ (verse 12).

God strikes his hands together at their dishonest gain (verse 13). He will scatter them among the nations and purge their uncleanness, and they will know that he is the LORD (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
Nearly every charge comes from the part of the law concerned with Israel living as a holy people: honoring parents, protecting the foreigner, keeping the Sabbath, avoiding the forbidden sexual unions, refusing bribes and interest. For Ezekiel, a priest trained in these texts, the city's sins were a point-by-point reversal of its calling.

Blood is the thread through the list, because shed blood was believed to pollute the land itself. Jeremiah, preaching inside the city in the same years, brought the same charges.

Notice the last charge in verse 12. Forgetting God is not a separate sin at the end of the list. It is the root of all the others.
passages.later: The law warned that bloodshed pollutes the land (Numbers 35:33). Jeremiah told the city to stop oppressing ‘the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow’ (Jeremiah 7:6).
passages.asks: Every sin on the list began with forgetting God. Ask where forgetting him appears first in your own life. And ask who around you is vulnerable and easily overlooked.

passages.t: Dross in the furnace, and no one in the gap
passages.happening:
‘Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to Me’ (verse 18). God will gather them in Jerusalem as metal is gathered in a furnace, and melt them in the fire of his wrath (verses 19-22).

Every part of the nation has failed. ‘The conspiracy of the princes in her midst is like a roaring lion tearing its prey’ (verse 25). The priests do violence to God's law and make no distinction between holy and common (verse 26). The officials are like wolves (verse 27). The prophets whitewash it all with false visions (verse 28). The people of the land oppress the poor and needy and exploit the foreigner (verse 29).

‘I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Silver was refined by melting ore and blowing air across it, so that the base metals separated out as dross and the silver was left. Ezekiel turns the picture around: when Israel is put in the furnace, there is no silver to recover.

The portrait of the leaders closely follows Zephaniah, written a generation or two earlier under Josiah. Nothing has changed. The people of the land were usually the landowning citizens of Judah, and they too have joined in oppressing the poor.

Standing in the gap was a picture of intercession: a person who stands in a broken wall to defend the city, as Moses once stood before God for Israel.
passages.later: Zephaniah had said, ‘Her princes are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves’ (Zephaniah 3:3). Jeremiah was told to search Jerusalem for ‘a single person, anyone who acts justly’ (Jeremiah 5:1).
passages.hard:
God says he found no one to stand in the gap, but Jeremiah was in Jerusalem in those years. Was there really no one?

Readers have noticed the problem. Jeremiah was a faithful prophet in the city, and others, such as Baruch and Ebed-melech, are presented as faithful too. Many take verse 30 as a prophet's way of speaking of the whole: the society, its leaders and institutions, had no one able to turn it. Others note that the person sought is someone with the standing to repair the wall, a leader who could turn the nation, which Jeremiah, persecuted and imprisoned, was not allowed to be. Others point out that God had told Jeremiah himself not to pray for this people, a sign that the time for prayer to avert the disaster had passed.

The chapter does not deny that faithful people existed. It says that none could stand in the breach and turn the city from its course.
passages.asks: God looked for one person to stand in the gap. Ask where there is a gap in your family, church or town that needs someone to pray and act. And ask whether you might be that person.
